The `here` package helps manage file paths in projects 
by automatically finding the project root and building paths relative to it:

```r
library(here)

# Automatically finds project root and builds paths
data <- readr::read_csv(here("data-raw", "survey.csv"))
saveRDS(results, here("inst", "analyses", "results.rds"))
```

This solves the problem of different working directory paths across collaborators. 
For example, one person might have the project at `/home/oski/Some-R-Project` while another has it at `/home/bear/R-Code/Some-R-Project`. 
The `here` package handles this automatically.

This works regardless of where collaborators clone the repository. 
For more details, see the [here package vignette](https://github.com/jennybc/here_here).

### Pass subpath components directly to `here()` {#sec-here-subpath}

`here::here()` already accepts path components as arguments
and joins them with the project root.
Do not wrap `here::here()` in `file.path()` or `fs::path()`:

```r
# Good: pass subpath components directly
rds_path <- here::here("inst", "extdata", "mapping.rds")

# Bad: redundant wrapping adds noise and defeats the purpose
rds_path <- file.path(here::here(), "inst", "extdata", "mapping.rds")
rds_path <- fs::path(here::here(), "inst", "extdata")
```

The wrapped form is functionally equivalent
but harder to read and obscures the intent.
`here()` was designed to replace `file.path()` for project-relative paths,
so let it do its job.

*See also @sec-here-package-practices for detailed explanation of the here package.*
